title: Petra and the Protocol
premise: Rosalind Thornbury, a veteran navigator who keeps the cryo-preserved 'backups' of dead crewmates in her cargo hold as a private penance, is docked at Petra Station when its governing AI, Protocol, begins broadcasting confessions to atrocities the war's victors buried. Hunted by both fleets, Rosalind and her estranged co-pilot Idris must carry Protocol's final message — proof that the war was manufactured by the Concord's founding families — across contested space. Betrayed by the resistance cell they trusted and forced to choose between destroying the message to save the backups' lives or delivering it to end the war, Rosalind realizes the backups were never cargo: they are witnesses. In the end she wakes them, lets them testify, and pays for it with her ship, her freedom, and Idris's love — but the truth lands, and the war collapses into reckoning.
about_author: Mara Coldharbour is the pen name of a former maritime radio operator who spent a decade listening to ships talk to each other in the dark. She writes about people who keep secrets in machines, and lives off-grid with two unreliable cats.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sleeping Cargo
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Docked at Petra Station, she runs her quiet ritual of checking on the eleven cryo-pods in her hold — crewmates who died under her command — while hauling a routine contract. Emotional beat: guilt worn smooth by habit, until a station-wide alert interrupts her.

chapters.title: Protocol Speaks
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. The station AI begins reading aloud, unprompted, a confession to the Meridian Bay massacre — an event officially blamed on the enemy fleet. Passengers panic; station security goes silent. Idris, who trusts machines more than people, recognizes the voice as genuine. Beat: dread mixed with vindication.

chapters.title: Confession Number Two
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Protocol confesses to falsifying the casualty records that started the war, naming the Concord's founding families. Rosalind realizes her brother died in one of the erased engagements. The station locks down around her ship. Beat: grief reigniting into purpose.

chapters.title: Eleven Names
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Rosalind's POV. Fifteen years earlier: the accident that killed her crew, the order she followed that caused it, and why she kept the bodies instead of returning them. Beat: the reader learns her penance has a hidden clause — she signed a silence agreement.

chapters.title: The Message
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Protocol transmits a sealed data-burst directly to Rosalind's ship, calling her by name: 'You have carried the dead long enough. Carry this.' It contains the full archive of manufactured evidence. Beat: terror and terrible honor; she cannot refuse without becoming complicit.

chapters.title: Dock Fees in Blood
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. Concord marines board Petra Station hunting the AI's chosen courier. Idris buys their escape window by sabotaging the docking clamps, stranding his own cousin among the marines. Beat: loyalty tested against survival; first fracture between him and Rosalind over methods.

chapters.title: Running the Contested Orbits
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A white-knuckle transit through the Kestrel Debris Field, dodging both fleets, with Protocol's fragmenting voice guiding them from the station's dying relay. Beat: intimacy of trust rebuilt mid-crisis; Rosalind and Idris fall back into old rhythm.

chapters.title: What the Backups Dream
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, night watch. Alone with the pods, she reads Protocol's archive and finds her own name in it — her silence agreement was part of the original cover-up. Beat: betrayal by her younger self; the penance she chose was designed to keep her quiet.

chapters.title: The Ashfall Cell
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. They reach the resistance stronghold at Ashfall, expecting sanctuary. The cell's leader, Veyra, welcomes them warmly — too warmly — and asks precise questions about the archive's structure. Beat: unease beneath hospitality; the reader sees the trap before they do.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Veyra proposes broadcasting only half the archive — enough to discredit the Concord, not enough to implicate the resistance's own founders. Rosalind refuses. Beat: idealism colliding with politics; the theme of truth vs. loyalty made explicit.

chapters.title: Locked Hold
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. Overnight, the Ashfall cell seals Rosalind's ship and seizes the pods, calling them 'collateral assets.' Idris discovers Veyra plans to trade the archive back to the Concord for amnesty. Beat: cold fury; he chooses Rosalind over his own movement.

chapters.title: The Long Way Out
chapters.summary: Dual POV. A sabotage-and-stealth escape through Ashfall's maintenance spines, using the station AI's ghost-protocols still resident in their ship. Beat: breathless action; Idris and Rosalind finally say aloud what they mean to each other, badly, mid-firefight.

chapters.title: Interdict
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Both fleets converge on their exit vector; a Concord admiral offers full pardons if they surrender the archive intact and unexamined. Beat: temptation offered politely; Rosalind hears her own fifteen years of silence echoed in the offer.

chapters.title: Fuel Is Truth
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. Stranded at a derelict refinery, they cannibalize parts and confront the arithmetic: they can power the pods or the transmitter home, not both. Beat: the central choice sharpened into machinery; love against duty rendered in kilowatts.

chapters.title: Veyra's Ghost
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Veyra catches up alone, unarmed, and confesses her own buried crime — she helped bury the Meridian evidence years ago out of fear. She gives them the last decryption key. Beat: mercy as strategy; enemies revealed as fellow prisoners.

chapters.title: The Waking
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Rosalind makes her decision: she begins reviving the backups, because the dead are the only witnesses no faction can discredit. One pod fails. Beat: devastating cost; the eleventh name is the one she loved most.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The revived crew, groggy and grieving, record their testimony into the archive — including the order Rosalind followed, implicating herself. Beat: catharsis through accountability; she stops being the archive's carrier and becomes part of it.

chapters.title: The Broadcast Window
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. They reach the neutral relay at Ceres Deep with a six-minute transmission window before Concord interdiction. Protocol's remnant consciousness, uploaded from Petra's ruins, arrives to co-sign the message. Beat: taut countdown; every theme converging.

chapters.title: Six Minutes
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The broadcast runs — names, dates, forged orders, her own signature on the silence agreement. Fleets go silent channel by channel. Then the Concord flagship opens fire on the relay. Beat: triumph curdling instantly into siege.

chapters.title: What Burns
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The ship is destroyed covering the relay's escape burst; Rosalind and Idris eject separately into the debris field, losing contact. Beat: sacrifice without guarantee; the darkest hour, written in silence and static.

chapters.title: Reckoning
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Rescued by defecting crews, they watch tribunals convene; the founding families fall, Veyra testifies, Protocol's final log is read into the record. Rosalind faces charges for her own role and does not ask for leniency. Beat: justice that costs everyone something.

chapters.title: Petra and the Protocol
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, epilogue. Years later, pardoned but un-promoted, she visits the memorial where the eleven names — now twelve, counting hers — are carved. Idris waits at the dock with a new ship and an old question. Beat: quiet hope; love surviving duty, choosing itself at last.
